title: Catholic: the Hail Mary
hook: a prayer drawn from the angel's and Elizabeth's words to Mary (Luke 1:28, 1:42)

segments.voice: Yesterday: lectio divina, one verse read four times. Your line was read slowly.

Two women, one old and one very young, both unexpectedly pregnant. The younger one has just traveled into the hill country to see her older cousin. She walks through the door, says hello, and before she can explain anything, the older woman cries out a blessing, and the baby in her own womb leaps. The younger one is Mary. The older one is Elizabeth. Part of what Elizabeth cried out that day is still prayed by Catholics, over and over, in one short prayer: the Hail Mary.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, BOTH EXPECTING.` → `THE BABY LEAPS.` → `STILL PRAYED TODAY.`

segments.voice: The Hail Mary is built like a mosaic, from pieces of Luke's Gospel. The first piece comes from the angel Gabriel, who visits Mary in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims translation, the Catholic English Bible: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." The second comes from Elizabeth, a few verses later: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Put them together, add the name Jesus, and you have the first half of the prayer, all of it straight from scripture. The second half, added later in the Church's history, is a request: Mary, the mother of God, is asked to pray for us, now and at the hour of our death. Today's line, full of grace, comes from a single Greek word Gabriel uses, kecharitomene. You can hear charis inside it, grace, from the week with Christianity. It means something like one who has been graced, favored, filled with favor. The King James Version translates it "highly favoured"; Catholic translations, following Latin, say full of grace. Catholic teaching honors Mary as the mother of Jesus and asks her prayers, as it asks the saints'; Catholics are clear that they don't worship her. Orthodox Christians have a similar prayer that also begins with the angel's greeting. In Protestant churches Mary is honored as a model of faith, and Luke's words are read rather than prayed. For Catholics it's a prayer learned in childhood, and repeated ten times in each decade of the rosary.
screen: `THE ANGEL: HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `ELIZABETH: BLESSED ART THOU.` · `THEN A REQUEST: PRAY FOR US.` · `KECHARITOMENE — FILLED WITH FAVOR.` · then, large: `FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Read the old greeting once, slowly: hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; if you pray, you can pray it, and if not, just listen to it as words. Then think of someone who has been full of grace toward you, someone who gave more kindness than you earned, and hold them in mind for a few breaths.
Catholic, through the Hail Mary: a prayer built from the angel's and Elizabeth's greetings to Mary, then a request for her prayers. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace. It began as greetings: an angel's, and a cousin's at the door. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics learn the Hail Mary as children and pray it on its own, in the rosary, and in the Angelus; its first half comes from Luke's Gospel and its second half asks Mary to pray for us.
